rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds.

The maximum CRF is already achieved, with substantial resolution margin. Shorten the gradient while holding temperature and endpoints fixed to test whether full resolution can be retained in less time.
Test the next shorter gradient to locate the resolution limit of the critical pair. Injection 2 remains a fully resolved, maximum-CRF fallback if this compression drops resolution below 1.5.

The critical pair loses resolution as the gradient steepens. Test higher temperature at the same slope to assess whether altered selectivity restores full resolution while further reducing retention time.

Trim the low-organic portion of the successful 8-minute gradient while keeping a slightly shallower slope. This tests whether the critical pair can retain full resolution with earlier elution, avoiding the selectivity losses seen at 60 C.

Test an intermediate temperature to improve the critical middle-pair selectivity without approaching the early-pair co-elution seen at 60 C. Keep the trimmed gradient fixed to isolate the temperature effect.

Injection 6 already achieves maximum CRF in a short run. Test a much steeper gradient at lower temperature for a potentially faster separation with reordered middle peaks, while favoring separation of the early pair.

Explore the fast-gradient regime with a slightly steeper slope and moderate temperature. The steeper slope may improve the reordered middle pair, while warming may separate the late pair; injection 6 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Return to the fully resolved regime of injection 6, raising the starting organic fraction to shorten retention while reducing the slope to protect the critical middle pair. Check whether the early pair remains sufficiently retained and resolved.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 9 to recover the small middle-pair resolution deficit. The narrower gradient window should still contain the last peak and may yield a faster fully resolved method than injection 6.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to preserve middle-pair separation. Lowering temperature should help retain and separate the early peaks, which are becoming limiting at 50 C.

Explore whether a higher starting organic fraction creates useful selectivity in the fast-gradient regime, where the middle pair remains limiting. Use 25 C to counter early-peak loss of retention, retaining injection 10 as the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Increase the starting organic fraction one step to test whether initial-solvent selectivity improves the unresolved middle pair in injection 12. Monitor the early pair closely because its retention and resolution will likely decrease.

Reduce the gradient slope at the promising high-organic starting condition to test whether the middle-pair deficit can be recovered. The lower endpoint should still elute all six compounds quickly, while the early pair retains its current resolution margin.

Further flatten the gradient at the same starting composition and temperature, since injection 14 improved the critical middle pair. The final hold may extend late-peak retention, but could deliver full resolution faster than injection 10.

The middle pair responds only weakly to further slope reduction at phi0 0.40. Test one higher starting-organic step for a selectivity gain and faster elution, while checking whether the early pair still meets R ≥ 1.5.

Return near the successful 50 C conditions, lowering the starting organic fraction to protect early-pair resolution while steepening the gradient to accelerate the last peak. Test whether this balance gives full resolution faster than injection 10.

Test temperature selectivity in the high-starting-organic regime, where changing slope alone did not fully resolve the middle pair. Compare directly with injection 14 to see whether warming improves that pair before the early pair becomes limiting.

Refine near injection 6 with a slightly steeper gradient and a trimmed endpoint that remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition. This tests whether its small resolution margin permits a faster maximum-CRF separation.

Lower the endpoint one grid step from injection 19 to recover full middle-pair resolution with a modest time increase. This should provide a short maximum-CRF method with more resolution margin than injections 6 and 10.

Test a shorter gradient ending near the last peak’s estimated elution composition, followed by the final hold. This explores whether hold-phase selectivity can preserve full resolution while reducing the separation time relative to injection 10.

Bracket temperature around the fastest fully resolved method, injection 10, while holding its gradient fixed. This tests whether a modest temperature reduction improves the early-pair margin without sacrificing middle-pair resolution.

Refine injection 10 by lowering the endpoint one step to improve the critical middle-pair resolution margin. This should retain maximum CRF with all peaks comfortably within 10 minutes, providing a more robust alternative to the fastest fully resolved method.

Combine the stronger early-pair separation at phi0 0.20 with a shallower slope than injection 20 to improve the middle-pair margin. This targets another maximum-CRF method with balanced resolution margins and all six peaks well within 10 minutes.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 10 to strengthen its critical-pair margin while keeping retention close to the fastest fully resolved result. Maximum CRF is already secured; this final refinement targets a short separation with modest additional resolution margin.
